title: Behold the man (John 19:1–5)
hookLine: crowned with thorns and shown to the crowd

lines: ONE SCENE, PAINTED AGAIN AND AGAIN.
THORNS, A CLOAK, A POINTING HAND.
cards: Two Latin words label a scene that painters kept coming back to. A man with his hands bound, a crown of thorns, a red or purple cloak hanging off his shoulders, sometimes a reed in his hand like a fake scepter.
Next to him, a man in fine clothes, pointing. Below, faces in a crowd. Titian painted it.
So did Caravaggio. It hangs in churches and galleries, one version after another. Those two words come from today's few verses.

teach.b: Pilate has found no case against Jesus. He offers to release him, and the crowd outside calls for Barabbas instead. So Pilate has him scourged.
Then the soldiers turn it into a game. They plait a crown out of thorns and press it on his head.
They throw a purple garment over him, a mock king's robe, and come up to him again and again saying, hail, king of the Jews, and strike him. Then Pilate walks him out in front of the crowd.

teach.h: A CROWN OF THORNS, A PURPLE CLOAK.
teach.b: In the Douay-Rheims: "Jesus therefore came forth, bearing the crown of thorns and the purple garment. And he saith to them: Behold the Man."
In Latin, Ecce homo. What did Pilate mean? Maybe, look at him, he's harmless, he's had enough.
Maybe contempt. John doesn't say. But Christians have heard more in it than Pilate meant.
Behold the man: not just this man, but what a human being looks like when he has been mocked and stripped of everything, and still is who he is.
The Church sees there, too, the servant Isaiah described, in the Douay: "Despised, and the most abject of men." That's part of why painters kept coming back to it.
It asks the viewer to do what Pilate asked the crowd: look, and don't look away.
Look at the man in the purple rag and see a person, a king even, in the one everyone is laughing at.

how: Catholics meditate on the crowning with thorns in the third Sorrowful Mystery of the rosary, and on Jesus's condemnation at the first Station of the Cross.

o: hail, king, the soldiers' mocking cry
behold the man, Pilate's words to the crowd
a cry for mercy from the crowd

games.q: behold the man — tap the pairs.

s: John tells us exactly what Pilate meant by behold the man
John doesn't say; it may have been pity, contempt or both.
Ecce homo is the Latin Vulgate's wording of John 19:5
the two words that label many paintings of the scene.
the crowning with thorns is one of the rosary's mysteries
the third of the Sorrowful Mysteries.

games.q: you're Pilate. you've had a prisoner whipped and mocked, and you think you've found no case against him. you bring him out to the crowd. what do you say?
o: I wash my hands of him.
games.why: at this moment he says, behold the man. 'behold your king' comes a little later (19:14), and the hand washing is in Matthew.

practice: Bring to mind someone who has been humiliated recently: a clip passed around online, a kid laughed at in class, a coworker embarrassed in a meeting, a stranger on the news.
Picture their face, not the joke, and hold your gaze there gently, the way you'd look at a friend.
If you pray, hold the words, behold the man, and see Christ in that face; if you don't, simply see a person and let your look be kind.

wordCard.voice: Ecce Homo. Latin for behold the man: Pilate's words as he shows Jesus, crowned with thorns, to the crowd. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: behold the man (John 19:5). The Latin Vulgate: ecce homo.

carryVoice: Your line: look with compassion. A person, never just the joke. Day five hundred twenty-eight, done.
